newsitem.title: NEPAL: Frenchmen say met missing German climber on Everest.
newsitem.headline: Frenchmen say met missing German climber on Everest.

text.p: Two Frenchmen said on Wednesday they may have been the last people to have met a German climber missing on the Tibetan side of Mount Everest since last week.

Antoine de Choudens and Stephane Cagnin, part of a French-Bulgarian expedition, said they met German Peter Kowalzik at 1 p.m. (0715 GMT) on May 8 while he was on his way up and they were descending from the top of the world's highest mountain.
Kowalzik, 29, a banker from Ludwigshafen, is one of three climbers missing on the northern face of the 8,848-metre (29,028-foot) peak since last week. He was climbing alone.
Two climbers died last week -- Alexandre Torochin, a Russian member of a Kazakh expedition, and a Nepali guide with a Korean expedition, Mingma Tamang.
Two members of the Kazakh expedition went missing during their descent from the Everest summit.
The French climbers told Reuters in the Nepali capital Kathmandu that they thought they must have been the last people to talk to Kowalzik.
They said they met him at the bottom of the ladder that helps climbers up a rock formation known as the Second Step, on the north ridge of Everest.
The Second Step, at 8,568 metres (28,110 feet), is the standard route to the Everest summit from the Tibetan side.
The Frenchmen said they chatted with Kowalzik, who congratulated them on their success, and they wished him good luck.
"He said he was fine," said de Choudens, 37. "He looked tired but okay."
The two climbers, who were due to leave for France later on Wednesday, said they were impressed by the fact that Kowalzik was not using oxygen.
They said it would have taken him about three hours to reach the summit.
"If he reached the top, he would have done so in very strong winds and much cloud," de Choudens said.
Both Frenchmen saw one body at 8,450 metres (27,723 feet), covered with snow, and said it could have been a climber who died last year.
Last May, three Indians were killed on the Tibetan side and five climbers died in blizzards on the Nepali side of Everest.
The Frenchmen also saw another body at 8,700 metres (28,543 feet) that was not covered with snow, and said it could have been someone who died very recently.
"He had obviously fallen because his head was down and legs were up," de Choudens said.
